inventory.name: JS Self-Profiling API in dedicated workers — Chrome 147 developer-trial extension that lets worker scripts collect their own call-stack samples, previously main-thread only
Profiler interface — the JS Self-Profiling API surface extended into dedicated workers (spec: [Exposed=(Window, Worker)], extends EventTarget)
new Profiler(options) with ProfilerInitOptions { sampleInterval (ms between samples), maxBufferSize (max samples before auto-stop) }
Profiler.stop() — awaited call that stops the session and returns the collected trace
ProfilerTrace — the returned trace object with stacks and frames (spec dictionary: resources, frames, stacks, samples), JSON-serializable

syntax.rationale: The capability has no declaration grammar of its own — it is the existing Profiler construction form executed in a dedicated worker script, which is exactly what the example block shows (comment: 'Inside a dedicated worker script (requires flag in Chrome 147)') followed by new Profiler({...}).

inputs.rationale: The example block documents the two configuration inputs a worker script passes: sampleInterval (ms between samples) and maxBufferSize (max samples before auto-stop).

outputs.rationale: The why-it-exists section states the output: 'statistical call-stack samples of their own execution ... structured JSON-compatible traces', letting engineers 'measure exactly where worker CPU time is spent'.

errors.rationale: The page documents no failure mode for worker-side self-profiling: the at-a-glance table records status, lineage, flag and spec links but no exception or error state, and the example shows only the success path. The WICG draft (fetched 2026-10-06) does define error behavior the page omits — RangeError for negative sampleInterval, NotAllowedError DOMException when Document Policy withholds permission, InvalidStateError DOMException from stop() on a stopped session, and the samplebufferfull event.

context.rationale: The at-a-glance table gives the execution context: dedicated workers in Chrome 147 as developer trial behind the enable-experimental-web-platform-features flag, extending an API 'available on main thread since Chrome 94'.

lifecycle.rationale: The example documents the session cycle: construction starts sampling, the buffer auto-stops at maxBufferSize ('max samples before auto-stop'), and the explicit awaited stop() ends the session and yields the trace.

examples.rationale: The example block is a runnable worker-script profile-then-stop flow with postMessage of the resulting trace.

compatibility.rationale: The at-a-glance table carries the compatibility row set: Chrome 147 developer-trial status, the flag name, the main-thread lineage, and links to the spec and ChromeStatus entry.

securityPrivacy.rationale: The page documents no security or privacy considerations: the why-it-exists section motivates the capability purely on measurement grounds, and no section records a policy gate — while the WICG draft (fetched 2026-10-06) gates the constructor on the js-profiling-mode Document Policy and suppresses stack frames from cross-origin scripts, and the ChromeStatus summary (fetched 2026-10-06) states the feature 'remain[s] gated by Document Policy'.

syntax.rationale: The interface's author-facing syntax is its construction form new Profiler({...}), the first statement of the example block; the spec declares it as constructor(ProfilerInitOptions options) on [Exposed=(Window, Worker)] EventTarget.

inputs.rationale: The ProfilerInitOptions inputs are shown in the example with their semantics in comments: sampleInterval 10 ms between samples, maxBufferSize 10_000 max samples before auto-stop (both required per the spec dictionary).

outputs.rationale: The example shows the interface's output value: the awaited trace from stop(), a ProfilerTrace object with stacks and frames, shipped out of the worker via postMessage.

errors.rationale: The page documents no interface-level error surface — the at-a-glance table lists status, lineage, flag and spec links only; the spec's RangeError/NotAllowedError/InvalidStateError behavior (fetched 2026-10-06) is not carried onto the page.

context.rationale: The at-a-glance table records where the interface is available: dedicated workers in Chrome 147 behind the experimental flag, extending the main-thread surface available since Chrome 94 (spec: exposed to Window and Worker).

lifecycle.rationale: The example shows the instance lifecycle: construct to start sampling, buffer-limited auto-stop, explicit awaited stop() to finish.

examples.rationale: One complete worker-script example exercises the interface end to end.

compatibility.rationale: The at-a-glance table's Status/Extends/Flag rows carry the Chrome 147 availability picture for the interface, with spec and ChromeStatus links.

securityPrivacy.rationale: No section of the page discusses access control or information exposure for the interface; the Document-Policy gate and cross-origin frame suppression defined in the spec (fetched 2026-10-06) are absent from the page's why-it-exists prose and everywhere else.

syntax.rationale: The example block opens with the page's strongest declaration grammar — new Profiler({ sampleInterval: 10, maxBufferSize: 10_000 }) — the full call form with both dictionary members the spec requires.

inputs.rationale: Both constructor inputs are documented with inline semantics: sampleInterval 'ms between samples' and maxBufferSize 'max samples before auto-stop'.

outputs.rationale: The example binds the constructed instance (const profiler = ...) which the page then uses to stop and collect the trace, documenting the constructor's output value.

errors.rationale: The page documents no constructor error behavior; the spec (fetched 2026-10-06) throws RangeError for negative sampleInterval and NotAllowedError DOMException when Document Policy denies js-profiling — none of which appears in the at-a-glance table or the example comments.

context.rationale: The constructor's context is fixed by the at-a-glance table: callable inside dedicated workers in Chrome 147 behind the enable-experimental-web-platform-features flag, where it was previously main-thread only.

lifecycle.rationale: The example documents that construction is the start of the sampling session, bounded by maxBufferSize auto-stop and ended by the explicit stop() call.

examples.rationale: The example block's first statement is a complete constructor invocation.

compatibility.rationale: Constructor availability follows the interface rows in the at-a-glance table: Chrome 147 developer trial behind a flag, main-thread surface since Chrome 94.

securityPrivacy.rationale: The page never states that construction is permission-gated; per the spec (fetched 2026-10-06) the constructor consults the js-profiling-mode Document Policy and can throw NotAllowedError, a consideration absent from the page's why-it-exists section and example.

syntax.rationale: The example documents the call form exactly as a reader writes it: const trace = await profiler.stop(); (spec: Promise<ProfilerTrace> stop()).

inputs.rationale: stop() is a nullary method and the page documents no arguments or per-call configuration for it — all parameterization lives in the constructor options shown earlier in the same example.

outputs.rationale: The example's awaited result is the method's output: a ProfilerTrace object with stacks and frames, assigned and then posted out of the worker.

errors.rationale: The page documents no error path for stop(); the spec (fetched 2026-10-06) rejects with InvalidStateError DOMException when the session is already stopped, a behavior absent from the at-a-glance table and the example.

context.rationale: The at-a-glance table places the method inside dedicated workers in Chrome 147 behind the experimental flag — the whole subject of the page's Extends row.

lifecycle.rationale: The example documents stop() as the explicit end of the sampling session — awaited after the workload, alternative to the maxBufferSize auto-stop.

examples.rationale: The example block contains the awaited stop() call in context.

compatibility.rationale: Method availability is the page's own subject: Chrome 147 developer trial in dedicated workers, per the at-a-glance table's status and flag rows.

securityPrivacy.rationale: The page documents no security or privacy dimension of stop() — the why-it-exists section frames it purely as the measurement endpoint; the spec's policy gating sits on construction (fetched 2026-10-06), which the page also does not mention.

syntax.rationale: There is no author-facing declaration grammar for ProfilerTrace — it is produced by stop(), not constructed by page code; the strongest honest fragment is the example block's call form that yields and consumes it (const trace = await profiler.stop(); postMessage({ trace })).

inputs.rationale: The trace's inputs are documented indirectly but concretely in the example: the samples the session collects between construction and stop(), bounded by the two constructor options.

outputs.rationale: The example comment documents the value's shape — 'trace is a ProfilerTrace object with stacks and frames' — and posts it out of the worker; the why-it-exists section adds that traces are structured and JSON-compatible.

errors.rationale: The page documents no error or invalid-trace handling for the returned value; the spec's buffer-full behavior (fetched 2026-10-06) — samplebufferfull event and transition to stopped — is not carried onto the page's at-a-glance table.

context.rationale: The example documents the trace's worker context and its exit path: produced inside the dedicated worker and transferred to the main thread with postMessage({ trace }).

lifecycle.rationale: The example documents the trace's lifecycle position: it exists once stop() resolves, after the workload and after any maxBufferSize auto-stop bound.

examples.rationale: The example block shows the trace being obtained and shipped in one flow.

compatibility.rationale: Trace production in workers rides the page's compatibility picture in the at-a-glance table: Chrome 147 developer trial behind a flag, per the status and flag rows.

securityPrivacy.rationale: The page documents no privacy treatment of trace contents, though a sampling trace embeds call-stack detail; the spec (fetched 2026-10-06) explicitly suppresses frames from cross-origin scripts with muted errors, a consideration the page never raises in its why-it-exists section or elsewhere.

notes: Source re-verification 2026-10-06, both cited sources linked by the page as required. (1) Gating divergence, neither side adjudicated: the page says the API is 'behind a flag in Chrome 147' via chrome://flags/#enable-experimental-web-platform-features and its at-a-glance table lists only that flag; the ChromeStatus record fetched 2026-10-06 confirms flag_name --enable-experimental-web-platform-features but its summary also states the feature 'remain[s] gated by Document Policy' with 'Document Policy support for workers tracked separately', and the WICG draft fetched 2026-10-06 has the constructor consult the js-profiling-mode Document Policy and throw NotAllowedError when not permitted. The two gates are not mutually exclusive but the page presents only one of them. (2) Status/milestone unverifiable from cited sources: the ChromeStatus API record fetched 2026-10-06 carries no populated impl_status or milestone fields and the milestone=147 listing query returned zero items, so the page's 'Chrome 147' and 'Developer trial' framing could not be re-confirmed — and no contradicting data was found. (3) The page's 'available on main thread since Chrome 94' claim is stated nowhere in either cited source as fetched 2026-10-06; it remains a page-only claim. (4) The page's example writes maxBufferSize as 10_000 where the spec examples write 10000 — cosmetic only.
